claim: Theta oscillations are one of the most prominent rhythms in the mammalian brain, with a frequency range of 4–12 Hz.
source: Theta oscillations (4–12 Hz) are one of the most prominent rhythms in the mammalian brain (Vanderwolf, 1969; Buzsáki et al., 1983; Colgin, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Vanderwolf, 1969; Buzsáki et al., 1983; Colgin, 2013) establishing theta oscillations as prominent brain rhythms.

claim: Theta is a distributed oscillation that is broadly coherent between the left and right hippocampi, the entorhinal cortex, the medial septum, and various other cortical and subcortical recipients of hippocampal projections.
source: Theta is a distributed oscillation, which is broadly coherent between the left and right hippocampi, the entorhinal cortex, the medial septum, and various other cortical and subcortical recipients of hippocampal projections (Buzsáki, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Buzsáki, 2002, which establishes the distributed and coherent nature of theta oscillations across brain regions.

claim: Neural activity is highly structured within each cycle of theta, with the firing rates of genetically defined cell types peaking at different phases.
source: Neural activity is highly structured within each cycle of theta, with the firing rates of genetically defined cell types peaking at different phases (Klausberger et al., 2003, 2004, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Klausberger et al., 2003, 2004, 2005, which documented phase-specific firing patterns of different cell types.

claim: Spatially selective principal cells in the hippocampus fire at progressively earlier phases of theta as animals traverse their individual place fields, a phenomenon known as phase precession.
source: Spatially selective principal cells in the hippocampus fire at progressively earlier phases of theta as animals traverse their individual place fields, a phenomenon known as phase precession (O'Keefe and Recce, 1993; Schmidt and Lipson, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to O'Keefe and Recce, 1993 and Schmidt and Lipson, 2009, which describe the phase precession phenomenon.

claim: The information content of hippocampal outputs changes throughout each cycle of theta.
source: Thus, the information content of hippocampal outputs changes throughout each cycle (Mehta et al., 2000, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mehta et al., 2000, 2002, which documented changes in information content across theta cycles.

claim: The degree to which other regions synchronize to the hippocampal theta rhythm is correlated with spatial decision-making performance.
source: The organization of activity relative to theta appears to be important for behavior, since the degree to which other regions synchronize to the hippocampal theta rhythm is correlated with spatial decision-making performance (Jones and Wilson, 2005; Sigurdsson et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Jones and Wilson, 2005 and Sigurdsson et al., 2010, which showed correlations between theta synchronization and performance.

claim: Theta could serve to coordinate cell assemblies such that encoded and retrieved information are less likely to interfere.
source: Theta could serve to coordinate cell assemblies such that encoded and retrieved information are less likely to interfere (Hasselmo et al., 2002; Hasselmo, 2005; Colgin and Moser, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hasselmo et al., 2002; Hasselmo, 2005; and Colgin and Moser, 2010, which proposed this theoretical framework.

claim: Input from the entorhinal cortex to the hippocampus is highest at the trough of theta waves recorded at the hippocampal fissure.
source: Input from the entorhinal cortex (EC), the major source of cortical projections to the hippocampus, is highest at the trough of theta waves recorded at the hippocampal fissure (Brankack et al., 1993; Kamondi et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Brankack et al., 1993 and Kamondi et al., 1998, which measured phase-specific input patterns.

claim: The hippocampus is more susceptible to long-term potentiation at the trough of theta waves recorded at the hippocampal fissure.
source: At this same phase, the hippocampus is more susceptible to long-term potentiation (Hyman et al., 2003; Kwag and Paulsen, 2009), consistent with the idea that this phase is optimized for encoding new information.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hyman et al., 2003 and Kwag and Paulsen, 2009, which demonstrated phase-dependent plasticity.

claim: At the peak of fissure theta, CA1 cells receive greater input from upstream cells in CA3.
source: At the 180° phase offset (the peak of fissure theta), CA1 cells receive greater input from upstream cells in CA3 (Hasselmo, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hasselmo, 2005, which described phase-specific input patterns from CA3.

claim: At the peak of fissure theta, stimulation of Schaffer collateral or temporoammonic inputs induces long-term depression.
source: At this phase, stimulation of Schaffer collateral or temporoammonic inputs induces long-term depression (Hyman et al., 2003; Kwag and Paulsen, 2009), which could suppress information storage during memory retrieval.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hyman et al., 2003 and Kwag and Paulsen, 2009, which demonstrated phase-dependent depression.

claim: High gamma oscillations (60–100 Hz) are a signature of enhanced coordination between CA1 and entorhinal cortex.
source: Simultaneously recording in CA1, CA3, and EC reveals that oscillations in the high gamma range (60–100 Hz) are a signature of enhanced coordination between CA1 and EC, whereas low gamma (25–50 Hz) indicates enhanced coordination between CA3 and EC.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Colgin et al., 2009, which demonstrated frequency-specific coordination patterns between hippocampal subregions and entorhinal cortex.

claim: Low gamma oscillations (25–50 Hz) indicate enhanced coordination between CA3 and entorhinal cortex.
source: Simultaneously recording in CA1, CA3, and EC reveals that oscillations in the high gamma range (60–100 Hz) are a signature of enhanced coordination between CA1 and EC, whereas low gamma (25–50 Hz) indicates enhanced coordination between CA3 and EC.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Colgin et al., 2009, which demonstrated frequency-specific coordination patterns.

claim: High gamma and low gamma oscillations occur at different phases of theta, and typically on different cycles.
source: Furthermore, these oscillations occur at different phases of theta, and typically on different cycles (Colgin et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Colgin et al., 2009, which documented the temporal separation of different gamma oscillations.

claim: The balance between the relative influence of the outside world (via EC) and internal states (via CA3) on hippocampal outputs is strongly modulated as a function of theta phase.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that the balance between the relative influence of the outside world (via EC) and internal states (via CA3) on hippocampal outputs is strongly modulated as a function of theta phase.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the preceding discussion of phase-specific input patterns from EC and CA3, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Task-dependent modulation of hippocampal firing is consistent with encoding of novel stimuli and retrieval of stored memories being biased to different phases.
source: Other studies have observed task-dependent modulation of hippocampal firing that is consistent with encoding of novel stimuli and retrieval of stored memories being biased to different phases (Manns et al., 2007; Lever et al., 2010; Douchamps et al., 2013; Newman et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Manns et al., 2007; Lever et al., 2010; Douchamps et al., 2013; and Newman et al., 2013, which observed phase-dependent encoding and retrieval patterns.

claim: Computational modeling studies provide support for the hypothesis that encoding and retrieval occur at different phases of theta.
source: Computational modeling studies provide further support for this hypothesis (Hasselmo et al., 2002; Hasselmo and Eichenbaum, 2005; Kunec et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to computational modeling studies by Hasselmo et al., 2002; Hasselmo and Eichenbaum, 2005; and Kunec et al., 2005.

claim: Parvalbumin-positive interneurons deliver fast and powerful inhibition to the cell bodies of pyramidal neurons in the hippocampus.
source: We directly activated parvalbumin-positive interneurons, which deliver fast and powerful inhibition to the cell bodies of pyramidal neurons in the hippocampus (Bartos et al., 2007), at either the falling phase or rising phase of theta recorded in the local field potential (LFP).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bartos et al., 2007, which characterized the properties of parvalbumin-positive interneurons.

claim: Four mice were trained on a spatial navigation task over the course of 2 to 4 weeks.
source: Four mice were trained on this task over the course of 2 to 4 weeks.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the experimental procedure performed by the authors.

claim: All mice expressed the gene for Cre-recombinase in parvalbumin-positive cells.
source: All mice expressed the gene for Cre-recombinase in parvalbumin-positive cells, to allow us to target expression of channelrhodopsin to these cells later in the experiment.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the genetic characteristics of the experimental animals.

claim: In the last 5 days of training, all mice performed at levels significantly above chance (p<0.05), with an average probability of correct response of 0.61 ± 0.05.
source: In the last 5 days of training, all mice performed at levels significantly above chance (p<0.05, based on p.d.f. of binomial distribution with chance level of 0.5), with an average probability of correct response of 0.61 ± 0.05 (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Mice increased the speed at which they performed the task to 1.49 ± 0.69 trials per minute during the last 5 days of training.
source: In addition to improving their accuracy, mice also increased the speed at which they performed the task, to 1.49 ± 0.69 trials per minute during the last 5 days of training (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: After at least 8 days of training, mice were implanted with a multielectrode array that targeted movable tetrodes and stationary fiber optic cables to hippocampus bilaterally.
source: After at least 8 days of training, mice were implanted with a multielectrode array that targeted movable tetrodes and stationary fiber optic cables to hippocampus bilaterally.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the experimental procedure.

claim: Two fiber optic cables (one per hemisphere) were implanted to a depth of 0.9 mm at the time of surgery.
source: Two fiber optic cables (one per hemisphere) were implanted to a depth of 0.9 mm at the time of surgery.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the surgical procedure.

claim: 1.0 µl of an adeno-associated virus carrying the gene for channelrhodopsin-2 was injected into both sides of the brain, centered on CA1 approximately 1 mm posterior to the septal pole of hippocampus.
source: In the same procedure, we injected 1.0 µl of an adeno-associated virus carrying the gene for channelrhodopsin-2 (Nagel et al., 2003) into both sides of the brain, centered on CA1 approximately 1 mm posterior to the septal pole of hippocampus.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the viral injection procedure, with a citation to Nagel et al., 2003 for the channelrhodopsin-2 construct.

claim: Expression of ChR2-EYFP spread at least 2 mm along the septotemporal axis, covering most of dorsal CA1 as well as overlying cortex.
source: Expression spread at least 2 mm along the septotemporal axis, covering most of dorsal CA1 as well as overlying cortex (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: All light pulses lasted 10 ms and had an irradiance of 50 mW/mm2 (∼2.5 mW from a 250 micron fiber optic cable).
source: All light pulses lasted 10 ms and had an irradiance of 50 mW/mm2 (∼2.5 mW from a 250 micron fiber optic cable).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the optogenetic stimulation parameters.

claim: Individual light pulses reliably elicited up to four spikes from well-isolated fast-spiking units (peak rate of 400 Hz).
source: Individual pulses reliably elicited up to four spikes from well-isolated fast-spiking units (peak rate of 400 Hz, Figure 2B–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2B-E.

claim: Nearby regular-spiking units were inhibited for a period of 25 ms following light onset.
source: Nearby regular-spiking units were inhibited for a period of 25 ms following light onset (Figure 2F), consistent with the known time constant of fast-spiking inhibition (Bartos et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2F and is consistent with prior knowledge cited from Bartos et al., 2007.

claim: The mean delay between the trigger event (peak or trough of theta reached) and the onset of the light pulse was 21.7 ± 7.2 ms for peak-triggered stimulation and 21.3 ± 7.4 ms for trough-triggered stimulation.
source: The properties of our closed-loop stimulation were as follows: the mean delay between the trigger event (peak or trough of theta reached) and the onset of the light pulse was 21.7 ± 7.2 ms for peak-triggered stimulation and 21.3 ± 7.4 ms for trough-triggered stimulation (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by timing data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The mean delay between trigger event and light pulse onset is equivalent to approximately 1/6 of a 125 ms theta cycle.
source: This is equivalent to approximately 1/6 of a 125 ms theta cycle.
evidence: The claim is a calculation based on the measured delay and the known duration of a theta cycle.

claim: The mean phase of stimulation (based on offline-filtered theta with no phase delay) was 96 ± 54° for peak-triggered stimulation and −131 ± 63° for trough-triggered stimulation.
source: The mean phase of stimulation (based on offline-filtered theta with no phase delay) was 96 ± 54° for peak-triggered stimulation and −131 ± 63° for trough-triggered stimulation (Figures 3E and 0° = peak).
evidence: The claim is supported by phase analysis data shown in Figure 3E (referenced as 3D in the text).

claim: The phase targeting for trough-triggered stimulation was less precise than for peak-triggered stimulation, as the rising phase of theta is shorter than the falling phase.
source: The phase targeting for trough-triggered stimulation was less precise, as the rising phase of theta is shorter than the falling phase (Belluscio et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Belluscio et al., 2012, which documented asymmetry in theta waveforms.

claim: The mean number of pulses per trial in the retrieval-stimulation condition (middle arm) was 8.8 ± 3.3 for peak-triggered stimulation and 8.3 ± 8.3 for trough-triggered stimulation.
source: The mean number of pulses per trial in the retrieval-stimulation condition (middle arm) was 8.8 ± 3.3 for peak-triggered stimulation and 8.3 ± 8.3 for trough-triggered stimulation.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement of measured stimulation parameters.

claim: For the encoding-stimulation condition, the mean number of pulses was 46.1 ± 57.2 for peak-triggered stimulation and 39.6 ± 39.6 for trough-triggered stimulation.
source: For the encoding-stimulation condition, the mean number of pulses was 46.1 ± 57.2 for peak-triggered stimulation and 39.6 ± 39.6 for trough-triggered stimulation (Figure 3D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D-F.

claim: Stimulation did not generally alter occupancy time in different segments of the track.
source: Stimulation did not generally alter occupancy time in different segments of the track (Figure 3G–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by occupancy time data shown in Figure 3G-H.

claim: On each trial, mice spent the majority of time in the encoding segment (average of 2–3 s for inbound trajectories and 5–8 s for outbound trajectories).
source: On each trial, mice spent the majority of time in the encoding segment (average of 2–3 s for inbound trajectories and 5–8 s for outbound trajectories).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement of measured behavioral data.

claim: Once mice left the sample arm, they ran quickly toward the goal, spending 1–2 s in the retrieval segment and a similar amount of time running toward the reward location after making their decision.
source: Once they left the sample arm, they ran quickly toward the goal, spending 1–2 s in the retrieval segment and a similar amount of time running toward the reward location after making their decision.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement of measured behavioral data.

claim: Optogenetic feedback altered the average power spectrum across trigger channels, for example by increasing the peak frequency and amplitude of theta during the peak-triggered stimulation condition.
source: Optogenetic feedback altered the average power spectrum across trigger channels, for example by increasing the peak frequency and amplitude of theta during the peak-triggered stimulation condition (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by power spectrum data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: There was an increase in power in the low-gamma band (25–35 Hz) for both peak and trough stimulation.
source: There was also an increase in power in the low-gamma band (25–35 Hz) for both peak and trough stimulation, but this was associated with a much stronger peak in the beta band (16–25 Hz), which may have affected the low-gamma band via spectral leakage.
evidence: The claim is supported by power spectrum analysis, with an inference about spectral leakage.

claim: Individual pulses affected the amplitude of subsequent cycles of theta, as evidenced by the difference in the mean LFP between −100 and −75 ms for actual vs dummy stimulation conditions.
source: Individual pulses affected the amplitude of subsequent cycles of theta, as evidenced by the difference in the mean LFP between −100 and −75 ms for actual (purple and teal) vs dummy (gray) stimulation conditions.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of LFP data comparing actual and dummy stimulation conditions.

claim: In 3/4 mice, trough-triggered stimulation occurred after the peak of high gamma, whereas peak-triggered stimulation occurred just after the trough of high gamma.
source: In 3/4 mice, we measured stimulation times relative to the peak of high gamma for both the trigger electrode and a neighboring electrode that was passively recording signals (Figure 4C). Although post-mortem analysis of electrolytic lesions revealed different locations for each electrode, all electrodes indicated that peak-triggered stimulation occurred just after the trough of high gamma, whereas trough-triggered stimulation occurred around or after the high gamma peak.
evidence: The claim is supported by phase analysis data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Despite variations in electrode location, absolute stimulation phase was similar across animals.
source: The consistency of this result indicates that, despite variations in electrode location, absolute stimulation phase was similar across animals.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the consistency of phase relationships across animals despite different electrode locations.

claim: High gamma power is a reliable indicator of enhanced coordination between CA1 and medial entorhinal cortex.
source: Although we did not measure CA1–MEC synchronization directly, previous studies have shown high gamma power to be a reliable indicator of enhanced coordination between these regions (Colgin et al., 2009; Yamamoto et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Colgin et al., 2009 and Yamamoto et al., 2014.

claim: When stimulation occurred in the retrieval segment, performance did not differ between baseline and peak-triggered stimulation for 4/4 mice (mean of 57.3 ± 10.0% correct for baseline vs 57.8 ± 10.5% correct for peak).
source: When stimulation occurred in the retrieval segment, performance did not differ between baseline and peak-triggered stimulation for 4/4 mice (mean of 57.3 ± 10.0% correct for baseline vs 57.8 ± 10.5% correct for peak, individual results in Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Table 1.

claim: For trough-triggered stimulation in the retrieval segment, performance improved significantly in 4/4 mice (71.0 ± 8.2% correct for trough).
source: For trough-triggered stimulation, however, performance improved significantly in 4/4 mice (71.0 ± 8.2% correct for trough; significance determined by the p.d.f. of the binomial distribution, with baseline accuracy for each mouse used as the 'chance' level).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data with statistical analysis using the binomial distribution.

claim: For stimulation in the encoding segment, performance during trials with trough-triggered stimulation did not differ from baseline in 3/4 mice (mean of 59.1 ± 2.4% correct for baseline vs 58.7 ± 10.5% correct for trough).
source: In this condition, performance during trials with trough-triggered stimulation did not differ from baseline in 3/4 mice (mean of 59.1 ± 2.4% correct for baseline vs 58.7 ± 10.5% correct for trough; 1 mouse had significantly impaired performance in the trough-stimulation condition).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data with statistical analysis.

claim: For peak-triggered stimulation in the encoding segment, performance improved significantly in 3/4 mice (mean of 69.6 ± 14.7% correct).
source: For peak-triggered stimulation, performance improved significantly in 3/4 mice (mean of 69.6 ± 14.7% correct; 1 mouse showed no difference from baseline).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data with statistical analysis.

claim: On average, trough-triggered stimulation resulted in a 13.7% improvement in accuracy for the retrieval condition, while peak-triggered stimulation resulted in a 10.5% improvement in accuracy for the encoding condition.
source: On average, trough-triggered stimulation resulted in a 13.7% improvement in accuracy for the retrieval condition, while peak-triggered stimulation resulted in a 10.5% improvement in accuracy for the encoding condition (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Trough-triggered stimulation improved performance more for the retrieval segment than the encoding segment in 4/4 mice.
source: The effects were consistent across individual mice, with trough-triggered stimulation improving performance more for the retrieval segment than the encoding segment in 4/4 mice, and peak-triggered stimulation improving performance more for the encoding segment than the retrieval segment for 3/4 mice (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Peak-triggered stimulation improved performance more for the encoding segment than the retrieval segment for 3/4 mice.
source: The effects were consistent across individual mice, with trough-triggered stimulation improving performance more for the retrieval segment than the encoding segment in 4/4 mice, and peak-triggered stimulation improving performance more for the encoding segment than the retrieval segment for 3/4 mice (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The probability that the same effects would be seen along any diagonal in the 2×2 experimental design was 0.0013.
source: The probability that the same effects would be seen along any diagonal was 0.0013.
evidence: The claim is based on bootstrap statistical analysis with 10,000 repetitions.

claim: The probability that the same effects were seen along both diagonals (what was observed in the actual data) was 0.0001.
source: The probability that the same effects were seen along both diagonals (what we observed in the actual data) was 0.0001.
evidence: The claim is based on bootstrap statistical analysis with 10,000 repetitions.

claim: Mice are much more likely to make a correct choice if they are cued to switch arms after failing to receive reward (82 ± 14% correct) or return to the same arm after receiving reward (72 ± 18% correct).
source: It is clear that the outcome of the previous trial has a strong effect on decision-making: mice are much more likely to make a correct choice if they are cued to switch arms after failing to receive reward (82 ± 14% correct) or return to the same arm after receiving reward (72 ± 18% correct; mean response across encoding and retrieval conditions, baseline trials only).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data analysis of baseline trials.

claim: Mice are less likely to switch arms after a correct decision (32 ± 9% correct) or to return to the same arm after an incorrect choice (40 ± 21% correct).
source: They are less likely to switch arms after a correct decision (32 ± 9% correct) or to return to the same arm after an incorrect choice (40 ± 21% correct).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data analysis of baseline trials.

claim: Mice exhibit a bias toward a 'win-stay, lose–switch' strategy.
source: Thus, mice exhibit a bias toward a 'win-stay, lose–switch' strategy.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the pattern of correct responses across different trial types.

claim: Trough-triggered stimulation in the retrieval segment improved performance on trials in which mice were cued to enter the opposite reward arm after making a correct choice by 19.5 ± 7.3%, with improvement seen in 4/4 mice.
source: The strongest effects were seen for trials in which mice were cued to enter the opposite reward arm after making a correct choice. On average, trough-triggered stimulation in the retrieval segment improved performance on these trials by 19.5 ± 7.3%, with improvement seen in 4/4 mice (versus 5.1 ± 14.7% for peak-triggered stimulation).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data analysis of specific trial types.

claim: Peak-triggered stimulation in the encoding segment improved performance on trials in which mice were cued to enter the opposite reward arm after making a correct choice by 25.0 ± 10.3%, with improvement in 4/4 mice.
source: Peak-triggered stimulation in the encoding segment improved performance on these trials by 25.0 ± 10.3%, again with improvement in 4/4 mice (versus 8.7 ± 14.6% for trough-triggered stimulation).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data analysis of specific trial types.

claim: There was no evidence for reduced performance by the 'optimal' stimulation phase for any trial type.
source: The effects of phase-specific stimulation on other types of errors were less pronounced, but there was no evidence for reduced performance by the 'optimal' stimulation phase for any trial type (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Triggering hippocampal inhibition on the peak of theta enhanced navigational accuracy when environmental cues to reward location are available (encoding segment).
source: When environmental cues to reward location are available (as in the encoding segment of the task), triggering hippocampal inhibition on the peak of theta enhanced navigational accuracy.
evidence: The claim summarizes the main experimental finding supported by the behavioral data.

claim: Triggering hippocampal inhibition on the trough of theta increased the probability of a correct choice when behavioral guidance must be based on internal signals alone (retrieval segment).
source: When behavioral guidance must be based on internal signals alone (as in the retrieval segment of the task), triggering hippocampal inhibition on the trough of theta increased the probability of a correct choice.
evidence: The claim summarizes the main experimental finding supported by the behavioral data.

claim: Phase-specific inhibition serves to reduce the response to task-irrelevant inputs.
source: Our favored explanation is that phase-specific inhibition serves to reduce the response to task-irrelevant inputs.
evidence: The claim is the authors' interpretation of their experimental results.

claim: On average, the influence of CA3 and entorhinal cortex inputs to CA1 changes as a function of theta phase.
source: On average, the influence of CA3 and entorhinal cortex inputs to CA1 changes as a function of theta phase (Hasselmo et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hasselmo et al., 2002.

claim: Parvalbumin-positive interneurons are typically active during the CA3-dominant phases of theta.
source: Although the parvalbumin-positive interneurons recruited by this manipulation are typically active during the CA3-dominant phases of theta (Lasztóczi and Klausberger, 2014), causal control allows us to activate them synchronously at arbitrary times during the theta cycle.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lasztóczi and Klausberger, 2014.

claim: Inhibiting CA1 during EC-dominant cycles in the retrieval segment improves task performance by increasing the relative influence of CA3.
source: Under the proposed mechanism, inhibiting CA1 during EC-dominant cycles in the retrieval segment improves task performance by increasing the relative influence of CA3.
evidence: The claim is the authors' proposed mechanistic explanation for their experimental results.

claim: Inhibiting CA1 during CA3-dominant cycles in the encoding segment improves task performance by increasing the relative influence of EC or by suppressing retrieval of interfering cross-trial information.
source: Conversely, inhibiting CA1 during CA3-dominant cycles in the encoding segment improves task performance by increasing the relative influence of EC or by suppressing retrieval of interfering cross-trial information.
evidence: The claim is the authors' proposed mechanistic explanation for their experimental results.

claim: Enhanced navigational accuracy could result from suppression of task-irrelevant information, rather than the enhancement of task-relevant information.
source: In both cases, enhanced navigational accuracy could result from suppression of task-irrelevant information, rather than the enhancement of task-relevant information.
evidence: The claim is the authors' interpretation of the mechanism underlying their experimental results.

claim: The duration of inhibition (∼25 ms) is equivalent to approximately 1/5 of a 125 ms (8 Hz) theta cycle.
source: The duration of this inhibition (∼25 ms) is equivalent to approximately 1/5 of a 125 ms (8 Hz) theta cycle, long enough to impact encoding or retrieval functions, but precise enough to avoid disrupting the entire cycle.
evidence: The claim is based on measured inhibition duration and calculation relative to theta cycle duration.

claim: The major cortical output of dorsal CA1 is retrosplenial cortex.
source: Besides projections back to the entorhinal cortex, the major cortical output of dorsal CA1 is retrosplenial cortex (Cenquizca and Swanson, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cenquizca and Swanson, 2007.

claim: Retrosplenial cortex is important for spatial working memory.
source: Retrosplenial cortex is known to be important for spatial working memory (Vann and Aggleton, 2004; Keene and Bucci, 2009; Vann et al., 2009), and changes in coupling between hippocampus and this region could affect performance on the present task.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Vann and Aggleton, 2004; Keene and Bucci, 2009; and Vann et al., 2009.

claim: There is a projection from CA1 to prefrontal cortex that originates primarily from the ventral regions.
source: There is also a projection from CA1 to prefrontal cortex, although this originates primarily from the ventral regions (Swanson, 1981; Cenquizca and Swanson, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Swanson, 1981 and Cenquizca and Swanson, 2007.

claim: Coupling strength between CA1 and medial prefrontal cortex depends on task phase.
source: Coupling strength between CA1 and medial prefrontal cortex is known to depend on task phase (Jones and Wilson, 2005), and it is therefore possible that phase-specific inhibition of CA1 could have a differential impact on CA1–mPFC synchrony during the encoding and retrieval segments.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Jones and Wilson, 2005.

claim: Mice could employ multiple strategies for completing the task, such as an egocentric, hippocampus-independent strategy based on turn direction or an allocentric, hippocampal-dependent strategy based on an internal map.
source: Mice could employ multiple strategies for completing the task, such as an egocentric, hippocampus-independent strategy based on turn direction or an allocentric, hippocampal-dependent strategy based on an internal map (Packard et al., 1989; Floresco et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Packard et al., 1989 and Floresco et al., 1997, which documented different navigation strategies.

claim: Baseline performance was modest at the start of testing, which makes it unlikely that a significant impairment could be observed, even if it did exist.
source: The fact that we instead observed only enhanced performance (rather than enhancement for one phase of stimulation and impairment for the other) may be explained by a floor effect. Baseline performance was modest at the start of testing (Figure 1A, Table 1), which makes it unlikely that we could observe a significant impairment, even if it did exist.
evidence: The claim is the authors' interpretation of why only performance enhancements were observed, based on baseline performance data.

claim: All mice were male parvalbumin-Cre (PV-Cre) heterozygotes, derived from PV-Cre BAC transgenics back-crossed into a C57BL/6J line.
source: All mice were male parvalbumin-Cre (PV-Cre) heterozygotes, derived from PV-Cre BAC transgenics back-crossed into a C57BL/6J line (Jackson Laboratory strain B6; 129P2-Pvalbtm1(cre)Arbr).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the experimental animals used in the study.

claim: Mice were 8–12 weeks old at the start of training (mean age = 10.8 ± 1.5 weeks) and 10–15 weeks old at the time of surgery (mean age = 13.5 ± 2.1 weeks).
source: Mice were 8–12 weeks old at the start of training (mean age = 10.8 ± 1.5 weeks) and 10–15 weeks old at the time of surgery (mean age = 13.5 ± 2.1 weeks).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the age of experimental animals.

claim: Animals were individually housed and maintained on a 12-hr light/dark cycle (lights on at 7:00 AM).
source: Animals were individually housed and maintained on a 12-hr light/dark cycle (lights on at 7:00 AM).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about animal housing conditions.

claim: All experimental procedures and animal care protocols were approved by the Massachusetts Institute of Technology Institutional Animal Care and Use Committees and were in accordance with NIH guidelines.
source: All experimental procedures and animal care protocols were approved by the Massachusetts Institute of Technology Institutional Animal Care and Use Committees and were in accordance with NIH guidelines.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about ethical approval for the study.
